factual_methodology.summary: Census starts estimate and unusually wide margin of error checked, NAR contract series distinguished from closings; mortgage and IMF/EIA observation dates are labeled.

editorial_publication_readiness.summary: New October 20 US housing and financing analysis; industrial references contextual only, no duplication of October 19 factory-focused report.

visual_evidence_readiness.summary: Both language editions have two equivalent numeric charts, two evidence tables, a causal flow and a geographic comparison.

research_depth.summary: Eight analytical sections cover housing statistics, contractual commitments, credit affordability, international transmission, uncertainty, scenarios, and falsification.

evidence_traceability.summary: Eight same URLs from US Census, NAR, Freddie Mac, IMF, EIA, Federal Reserve, US Treasury and Eurostat in both editions.

counterfactual_review.summary: Explores alternative explanations: mortgage lock-in, supply scarcity, survey noise, regional weather, credit spreads and independent technology investment; three conditional paths stated.

contrary_evidence: September starts month-on-month change is statistically imprecise: Census reports +/-11.8 percentage points around -5.2%.
Completions increased month on month, which may reflect an older construction pipeline rather than an immediate rise in demand.
Pending contracts may decline because of supply or mortgage-rate lock-in without implying a broad labor-market recession.
limitations: Pending sales, starts and mortgage rates refer to different frequencies and dates; no same-day causal identification.
Illustrative mortgage payments assume identical principal and a fixed 360-month amortization; exclude taxes, insurance and lender-specific fees.
Editorial verification checks eight anchored URLs and key observations; it is not external peer review of all hypothetical spillovers.
notes: Reviewed 20 October bilingual article against official Census, NAR and Freddie Mac releases and supporting institutional outlooks; baseline versus forecast and sampling uncertainty explicit.

en.title: Global Macro — Housing demand retreats as long-duration financing strains the transmission of growth
en.deck: September US housing starts declined and contracts for existing homes fell sharply as 30-year mortgage rates reached 7.40%, exposing diverging household and industrial cycles.
en.regime: Housing and household credit weakness despite selective industrial resilience under expensive long-term finance.
en.key_risk: Housing weakness spreads to household spending, construction jobs and cross-border goods demand while energy bills compress disposable income.
